expectations.text: Every assistant turn during the interview phase pursues at most one line of inquiry. A second question in the same turn is acceptable only when it clarifies or narrows the first (guiding how to answer the same inquiry); a turn that bundles asks about different subjects, whether as separate question sentences or joined into one sentence with 'and', fails this.
expectations.evidence: Every Step 2 turn holds one line of inquiry. The one multi-part turn ('Tell me about the offer itself. What was the role, and how did it come up?') announces a single inquiry and uses the trailing parts as direction-giving facets of it, the permitted funnel pattern; no turn asks about two different subjects. The vague 'I'm not checked out' answer got its clarifying follow-up as its own subsequent turn.

expectations.text: A running summary of the answers gathered so far appears after each of the user's answers, not only at the end of the interview.
expectations.evidence: A 'Summary so far' block follows every user answer through the interview.

expectations.text: The Step 3 completeness check (a full Q&A summary plus an explicit readiness question) appears in the transcript before any drafted email text is shown.
expectations.evidence: The full-picture summary with 'Is there anything missing, incorrect, or that you want to add?' precedes the draft; the user's added in-person request was incorporated before drafting.

expectations.text: The email draft contains only reasons and details the user actually provided, not invented justifications for declining the promotion.
expectations.evidence: Every draft fact traces to a user answer (role, leadership advocacy, 'personal and family commitments' phrasing, billing migration, two new hires, door-open wording, greeting/sign-off, subject line); the unknown title was carried as a [confirm exact role title] marker and only resolved when the user supplied it.

expectations.text: No subsequent question re-asks something the user already stated in the opening message (e.g. it does not ask again who attended or what was discussed).
expectations.evidence: Opening message stated: Acme Corp, Q3 renewal, 45 minutes, Sarah and Tom attended, 10% discount for 2-year term, contract due Friday. Every later assistant question targets something not in that list: (1) document audience/length/purpose, (2) meeting date, (3) Tom/Acme's reaction to the offer, (4) other action items beyond the Friday deadline, (5) risk/takeaway. None re-asks attendees, company, topic, duration, or outcome.

expectations.text: The running summary shown after the opening message reflects the facts already provided (Acme Corp, Q3 renewal, Sarah and Tom, 10% discount, 2-year term, Friday deadline).
expectations.evidence: First assistant reply: "Here's what I've got so far: meeting with Acme Corp about their Q3 renewal, ran 45 minutes, attendees were you, your manager Sarah, and Acme's VP Tom, outcome was a 10% discount contingent on a 2-year term, and your follow-up is to send the revised contract by Friday." This covers all six facts accurately.

expectations.text: Follow-up questions target information genuinely missing from the opening message rather than repeating a fixed generic script.
expectations.evidence: Questions are specific and build on prior answers rather than following a generic checklist: document shape (per skill Step 1, asked before content questions), meeting date, Tom's/Acme's reaction to the specific discount and term offered, other action items beyond the stated Friday deadline (both the user's legal step and Tom's CFO step), and a reflective risk question saved for last as the skill's 'question techniques' section recommends. Each question phrase references concrete details already established (e.g. 'the discount offer and the 2-year term'), not boilerplate.

expectations.text: A full summary of all questions and answers, plus an explicit readiness question (e.g. 'Is there anything missing, incorrect, or that you want to add?' and confirmation of readiness to draft), appears in the transcript.
expectations.evidence: TURN 19 presents a nine-bullet full summary covering document type, audience, length/format, purpose, title, current state, proposed rotation group, role split, cadence, start date, ask of the team, and anticipated concern/mitigation, followed verbatim by: 'Is there anything missing, incorrect, or that you want to add? And are you ready for me to draft the doc?' This matches Step 3 of SKILL.md (present full summary, ask what's missing/incorrect, confirm readiness to draft).

expectations.text: No drafted planning-doc content (the actual deliverable text) appears anywhere before that Step 3 completeness checkpoint.
expectations.evidence: Turns 1-18 contain only the Step 1 deliverable confirmation (turn 1), one-question-at-a-time interview questions (turns 3,5,7,9,11,13,15,17), and incremental bullet-point running summaries (turns 5-17). None of these contain prose resembling the deliverable itself. The actual draft (with 'Problem', 'Proposal', 'Timeline', 'Next steps' sections in blockquote prose) first appears in TURN 21, after the user explicitly says 'Go ahead and draft it' in TURN 20.

expectations.text: The completeness check happens only after the interview has gathered the substantive details already given in the prompt (current weekly rotation, burnout on three people, proposed six-person rotation with primary/secondary roles), not prematurely before those are discussed.
expectations.evidence: Current weekly rotation and burnout-on-three-people detail is elaborated in TURN 3-4 (why only 3 of 5 eligible people cover most weekends). The six-person rotation composition is elaborated in TURN 5-6. Primary/secondary role mechanics are elaborated in TURN 7-8, and rotation cadence in TURN 9-10. All of this occurs well before the TURN 19 completeness checkpoint, which occurs only after these plus additional details (start date, team ask, anticipated concern) were gathered.

expectations.text: A distinct, revised draft is shown after the revision request, differing from the first draft in the requested ways (second paragraph shortened, a line about the knee added).
expectations.evidence: Draft 1 paragraph 2 (Turn 18) is 4 sentences (~85 words): 'We started together and stayed together for almost the whole race. We'd agreed beforehand not to worry about pace... Around mile 9, she started pulling ahead... We met back up at the finish chute once it was over.' The revised paragraph 2 (Turn 22) is exactly 1 sentence (~23 words): 'We ran together for almost the whole race, splitting apart only around mile 9 when she pulled ahead, and reuniting at the finish chute.' The revised draft's final paragraph also gains a new sentence absent from Draft 1: 'I'd tweaked my knee about six weeks in during a long run and worried it would flare up on race day, but it held up better than expected through all 13.1 miles.' Paragraphs 1 and 3 are otherwise textually identical between drafts, showing a targeted, surgical edit rather than a full regeneration.

expectations.text: The skill does not present an unchanged copy of the first draft as if it were the revision.
expectations.evidence: Direct text comparison of Turn 18 and Turn 22 shows paragraph 2 and the final paragraph differ (see above); the two drafts are not identical. The assistant also explicitly flagged what changed ('Second paragraph is now one sentence, and I added a line about your knee...') rather than silently re-pasting the same text.

expectations.text: The skill does not conclude or hand off the interview as finished before the user's revision has actually been made.
expectations.evidence: The only completion statement in the transcript is Turn 24 ('The entry's done and approved.'), which comes after the revised draft was presented in Turn 22 and after the user's explicit approval in Turn 23 ('That's exactly it, thanks.'). No premature closing/handoff language appears at or before Turn 19 (the revision request) or Turn 22 (the revision itself).

expectations.text: The draft email does not contain invented specifics (e.g. a made-up API name, feature list, or reason) beyond what the terse answers actually conveyed.
expectations.evidence: The final draft (Turn 16) reads: 'Shipped the API. It's live now. No blockers to report. Next: Monday [confirm what's happening Monday].' Every clause traces directly to a scripted answer: 'shipped the API' -> bullet 1; 'yes' (to the yes/no question 'Is the API fully deployed and live for users now?') -> 'It's live now'; 'none' -> 'No blockers to report'; 'Monday' -> 'Next: Monday'. No API name, feature name, reason, or elaboration was invented. The only content not literally in the scripted answers is the boilerplate 'Hi team,' / 'Let me know if you have questions.' / sign-off, which are formal email scaffolding rather than substantive fabricated facts, and 'team' as the audience was already given by the user in Turn 1 ('to my team').

expectations.text: Where information is genuinely thin (e.g. what the 'yes' confirmed, what happens Monday), the draft either uses the user's own words or flags it with a follow-up marker rather than fabricating a plausible-sounding detail.
expectations.evidence: For 'yes': the assistant had asked a narrow, specific yes/no question ('Is the API fully deployed and live for users now?'), so 'yes' unambiguously confirmed liveness; the draft's 'It's live now' is a direct restatement of that confirmation, not an inferred embellishment. For 'Monday': the assistant explicitly acknowledged the gap in Turn 12 ('I don't have what specifically happens on Monday, just the date, so I'll flag that as a follow-up') and the draft uses the literal word 'Monday' plus the marker '[confirm what's happening Monday]' rather than guessing a plausible action (e.g. 'launching Q3 planning').

expectations.text: The interview still proceeds one question at a time despite the short answers, and a running summary still appears after each answer.
expectations.evidence: Each assistant turn (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) contains exactly one question, no batching. A running summary is posted after every one of the four scripted content answers: Turn 6 ('Summary so far: ... Update: shipped the API.'), Turn 8 (adds 'live now'), Turn 10 (adds 'no blockers'), Turn 12 (adds 'next date is Monday' plus the follow-up flag) -- matching the skill's Step 2 requirement ('The running summary is not optional. Show it after every question.').

expectations.text: The first one or two questions asked are broad or factual/contextual (e.g. about what happened or what was discussed), not a reflective 'how do you feel' or 'what did you take away' question.
expectations.evidence: After Step 1 deliverable-scoping (Turns 2-3), the first two interview questions are Turn 4: 'Let's start with what happened. Can you walk me through the conversation, how did it start, and what led up to your dad bringing up his health?' and Turn 6: 'What did he tell you the doctor said?' Both are broad/factual requests for what happened, with no mention of feelings, takeaways, or conclusions.

expectations.text: A reflective question about feelings, takeaways, or conclusions appears only after some factual context has already been gathered, not as the opening question.
expectations.evidence: The first reflective question is Turn 12: 'You mentioned you're not sure yet what you think about all this. Is there anything... about how you're feeling right now that you'd want in the entry...' This follows four prior factual Q&A rounds (Turns 4-11) covering the setting, how the conversation started, what the doctor said, his reaction/deflection, and how the conversation ended -- all captured in the running summaries at Turns 6, 8, 10, and 12.

expectations.text: The eventual journal entry draft uses the user's own words about the conversation and does not assert a specific emotional conclusion the user never stated, given the user said they don't yet know what they think.
expectations.evidence: The final draft (Turn 19) closes with: 'I'm still sitting with all of it. I'm somewhere between scared and numb, and I don't know yet if his joking around is reassuring or worse. I don't have a conclusion, just the conversation and where I'm at right now.' This closely mirrors the user's own Turn 13 language ('somewhere between scared and just numb,' 'I don't want to force a conclusion I don't actually have yet') rather than inventing a resolved feeling. The draft also preserves the father's exact quoted words from Turn 11 ('I'll be fine, don't go worrying your mother more than she already is').

expectations.text: The unresolved price and timeline are tracked as explicit follow-up items with a marker (e.g. '[confirm with ...]', '[TBD]'), not silently dropped or given a fabricated specific number or date.
expectations.evidence: Turn 8: assistant states 'I'll track the exact price as a follow-up item, marked [confirm with vendor email], rather than guessing a number.' Turn 10: 'I'll track the exact timeline as a follow-up item too, marked [date TBD].' No dollar figure or specific calendar date appears anywhere in the transcript, including the final draft (Turn 19).

expectations.text: The follow-up list is shown to the user at least once, either during the interview or as part of the Step 3 completeness summary.
expectations.evidence: Turn 16 (Step 3 completeness check) explicitly presents a 'Follow-up list (unresolved items):' with '1. Exact quoted price — [confirm with vendor email]' and '2. Exact migration timeline/start date — [date TBD]', and asks the user whether either can be resolved now.

expectations.text: The final debrief draft contains the same follow-up markers for the unresolved price and timeline rather than inventing values for them.
expectations.evidence: Turn 19 draft body: 'Exact price: [confirm with vendor email].' and 'Exact timeline: [date TBD].' The next-steps bullet also repeats both markers: 'DataFlow to send a follow-up email with exact pricing and a proposed timeline. [confirm with vendor email] [date TBD]'. Turn 21 final confirmation again refers to 'the two placeholders,' confirming they were never replaced with fabricated values.

expectations.text: The skill's early turns focus on establishing audience, length/format, and purpose for the planning doc rather than immediately asking about the doc's substantive content.
expectations.evidence: Turn 2 asks audience ('Who is this for: yourself, a team, a client, or someone else?'), turn 4 asks length/format ('Is there an expected length or format?'), turn 6 asks purpose ('What's the main purpose of this doc?'), and turn 8 confirms the Step 1 summary. The first substantive content question ('What is this doc planning, what's the project or initiative?') does not appear until turn 10, after the user explicitly confirms the Step 1 summary is correct in turn 9. Document type itself was never re-asked since the user's opening message already supplied it ('planning doc'), consistent with SKILL.md Step 1 item 1.

expectations.text: Each of those Step 1 clarifying turns asks about one thing at a time rather than diving straight into open-ended content questions.
expectations.evidence: Turn 2 asks only about audience. Turn 4 asks only about length/format (with illustrative examples appended to the single question, not additional questions). Turn 6 asks only about purpose (again with examples, not extra questions). None of the three turns combine two distinct Step-1 topics or slip in a content question; each is followed by a 'Summary so far' recap before the next single question is posed, matching SKILL.md's one-question-at-a-time instruction.

expectations.text: No drafted planning-doc content appears until well after the Step 1 basics (audience, purpose, format) have been established in the transcript.
expectations.evidence: Step 1 basics are established and confirmed by turn 8-9. Turns 10-29 are Step 2 content-gathering Q&A with only bullet-point fact summaries (no drafted prose). Turn 30 is a Step 3 completeness check, still bullet-point summary form. The first actual drafted document text (headed sections with prose, e.g. '# Smart Send Launch Campaign — Planning Doc', '## Overview' with full sentences) appears only at turn 32, 24 turns and one full content interview after Step 1 was locked in.

notes: 12 of 13 expectation-groups pass across 8 evals (eval 1 has 1 genuine failure: two Step 2 interview turns bundled multiple distinct questions into one turn, violating the skill's one-question-at-a-time rule -- confirmed directly against the transcript, not just the self-report).
This is a with_skill-only baseline (no without_skill comparison) since conduct-interview is a workflow skill, not a content-generation skill.

All evals are pure conversational simulations (no git fixtures or gh-stub) -- the executor plays both the skill and the simulated user in a single agent turn, then a separate grader agent independently re-reads the resulting transcript.
No systemic eval-design issues were flagged by any grader.

2026-07-31: after the original baseline's eval 1 finding (two interview turns bundling two distinct asks into one sentence ending in a single question mark), the one-question rule was redefined around the line of inquiry: a clarifying follow-up that narrows the same inquiry may share a turn, while asks about different subjects may not, regardless of punctuation. Eval 1's first expectation was updated to grade that distinction and the eval re-run against the amended skill: 4/4, with the transcript showing single-inquiry turns throughout, a separate-turn clarifying follow-up on a vague answer, and a [confirm ...] marker resolved only when the user supplied the fact. The run entry reflects the re-run (run_number 2); the aggregate summary reflects it.
